title: Finding Amanda
full_review:
The back streets of Las Vegas are the setting for the pungent, semi-autobiographical black comedy "Finding Amanda" (Magnolia).

Although he has beaten alcohol and drug abuse, floundering Los Angeles TV writer Taylor Mendon (Matthew Broderick) can't shake his gambling compulsion or the habitual lying to his wife Lorraine (Maura Tierney) that barely masks it. When she comes across a slew of recent racing stubs in their glove compartment, she reluctantly demands a separation.

Desperate to regain Lorraine's confidence, Taylor strikes on an unlikely plan. He'll drive to Sin City, where they've recently learned that their 20-year-old niece Amanda (Brittany Snow) is working as a prostitute -- presumably to finance her own drug habit -- and convince her to enter an upscale Malibu rehab clinic and demonstrate that he really can resist betting on the horses.

Predictably, every detail of this scheme goes awry. Taylor's first stop is his favorite casino's cash desk and, when he finally locates Amanda in a second-rate, Aztec-themed hangout on the wrong side of town, she's not particularly anxious to be rescued.

 

Taylor is shocked and discomfited by Amanda's clear-eyed preference for streetwalking over her previous job flipping pancakes at IHOP. His wincing reactions -- Broderick is a master of upended innocence -- and his disdain for her abusive live-in boyfriend Greg (Peter Facinelli) provide writer-director Peter Tolan's script with much of its comic artillery.

 

If her uncle looks askance at her choices, Amanda's eyes are wide open to his insatiable thrill-seeking, as graphically illustrated when she leaves an Ecstasy pill with him to test his resolve. This, together with his jocularly treated fall off the wagon, raises the obvious question: which of them is more in need of treatment?

 

Making his feature directing debut, Tolan, himself a TV director, has chosen some questionable topics for comedy, and the interludes of serious reflection, such as the two scenes in which Amanda -- once tearfully and later meditatively -- grapples with the reality of her situation, seem at odds with the generally flippant tone. But its factual origins and redemptive trajectory keep the film from ranking as sheer exploitation of its characters' self-destructive behavior.

The film contains nongraphic sexual activity, implied nonmarital sex and cohabitation, rear and upper female nudity, drug use, prostitution, strong sexual themes and humor, pervasive rough and crude language, several uses of profanity and obscene gestures. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
